Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

benefit verb

do good to, be good for

also benefit from, do good, it will do you good, who benefits?, be of use, beneficial, do a lot of good, it does a lot of good, be of service to someone, be good for, do someone good

classical

Hor. Ars 333: aut prōdesse volunt aut dēlectāre poētae
Plin. Ep. 7.21.3: balineum assūmō quia prōdest
Traupman 97: prōderit (multum, nihil) tibi, it will do you (a lot of, no) good
Cic. Tusc. 4.30.64: multum prōdest ea quae metuuntur ipsa contemnere (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 99: multum prōdesse
Traupman 305
Traupman 322

prōsum, prōdesse, prōfuī

verb, irregular (prō + sum), with the dative

do good, benefit, be of use (to)

The person helped goes in the dative: tibi prōderit, it will do you good. Lewis & Short: of medicines, “to be good, be beneficial”. The opposite is obesse or nocēre.

Other words

  • bonō esse — be to someone’s advantage; cui bonō? who benefits?

    phrase: the dative bonō with the dative of the person · also used · classical · Cic. Rosc. Am. 84: quaerere solēbat ‘cui bonō’ fuisset; Cic. Rosc. Am. 13: quibus occīdī patrem Sex. Roscī bonō fuit

    Lucius Cassius’s question in court, cui bonō fuisset?, “who stood to gain?”, which Cicero quotes again at Phil. 2.35, illud Cassiānum.

  • ūsuī esse — be of use, of service (to)

    phrase: the dative ūsuī with the dative of the person · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.1.3: fuit et mihi et Quīntō frātrī magnō ūsuī; Caes. BG 1.50: utrum proelium committī ex ūsū esset necne

    Also ex ūsū esse, to be of advantage (Caesar).

  • frūctum capere (ex) — benefit from, get the good of

    phrase: ex with the ablative of the thing one benefits from · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 1.9.20: cum sē maximum frūctum cēpisse dīcerent ex lībertāte meā; Traupman 269: derive great advantage from, multum commodum ex aliquā rē capere

    Frūctus is the produce of a field, and so the return one has from anything (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • aut prōdesse volunt aut dēlectāre poētae

    poets aim either to do good or to give pleasureHor. Ars 333

  • Balineum assūmō quia prōdest, vīnum quia nōn nocet, parcissimē tamen.

    I take a bath because it does me good, and wine because it does no harm, though very sparingly.Plin. Ep. 7.21.3

  • L. Cassius … identidem in causīs quaerere solēbat ‘cui bonō’ fuisset

    Lucius Cassius used to ask again and again in his cases ‘who benefited?’Cic. Rosc. Am. 84

  • quī ipse sibi sapiēns prōdesse nōn quit, nēquīquam sapit

    a wise man who cannot do himself any good is wise in vainEnnius in Cic. Fam. 7.6.2

See also advantage, help, healthy, interest.
